exposition: Interpret an inequality as a condition satisfied by a region of values. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In inequalities and truth sets, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Candidate points on a number line. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Truth-region shading. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

exposition: Derive point, interval, or exterior solutions from distance meaning. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In absolute-value equations and inequalities, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. exposition: Interpret an inequality as a condition satisfied by a region of values. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In inequalities and truth sets, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Truth-region shading. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

exposition: Translate among inequalities, number-line graphs, and interval notation. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. unit.title: Inequalities, Absolute Value, and Formulas
unit.act: Act III - Describing regions and constraints
unit.role: Extend algebra from exact equality to ranges, distance conditions, and reusable formulas.
unit.governingQuestion: How do we describe all values satisfying a condition?
unit.storyArc: Equation methods are adapted to inequalities; negative scaling reveals order reversal; intervals describe regions; absolute value becomes distance; formulas are rearranged without assigning numerical values.
outcomes: Interpret and graph inequality solution sets.
Explain why multiplication or division by a negative reverses order.
Translate among inequality, interval, and number-line forms.
Solve compound and absolute-value inequalities.
Rearrange formulas and preserve units.
unit.investigation: Represent manufacturing tolerance or acceptable measurement error in words, inequalities, intervals, graphs, and absolute value.
unit.mastery: Students solve, graph, and interpret mixed inequalities and rearrange formulas with units.
